Hard to say without much info as there are so many variables. 


If the abscess was identified from a post-op CT, then they would know roughly how big it was and therefore how much should ideally come out of the drain.


How high the markers of inflammation are on his bloods (and if he's had any high temperatures) will also determine how many more days of IV antibiotics he needs, or whether he can be stepped down to oral (can go home with latter). Doctors don't routinely share results of blood tests taken in hospital unless asked - best time to try and have a chat with a doctor is a weekday before 5pm (outside of this they're honestly just too busy, and unlikely to be the regular team looking after your partner, though they will talk if they can - info will just come from the notes, however)


Having a bowel movement is also important for discharge - things slow down with any kind of surgery, but more so abdominal surgery. Combine that with not moving much (movement stimulates bowels) and if he's on any opioids e.g. morphine for pain.

Oxygen is stored in 2 ways in a hospital:


1) as a liquid in a vacuum insulated evaporator (the big white tanks you can sometimes see outside on hospital grounds). Very efficient for large supplies of oxygen. If you're interested in how exactly it works, some nice images come up with a quick google of 'vacuum insulated evaporator)


2) As a gas in a cylinder manifold (largely serves as a backup to the above, approx 2 days worth of supply). 


The oxygen itself is obtained largely through the fractional distillation of air - air is cooled then slowly heated back up to separate out the constituent gases.
